chunks: Abu Ali Al-Ash'ari, from Al-Hasan ibn Ali Al-Kufi, from Ali ibn Mahziyar, from Uthman ibn Isa, from Ibn Muskan, from the one who reported it, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

Indeed, when Dawud (peace be upon him) took his stand at Arafat, he looked at the people and their multitude, so he ascended the mountain and turned to supplicate. When he had completed his rituals, Jibra'il (peace be upon him) came to him and said to him: 'O Dawud! Your Lord says to you: Why did you ascend the mountain? Did you think that the voice of one who speaks would be hidden from Me?'

Then he took him to the sea, to Jeddah, and caused him to descend into the water, traveling for forty mornings on land. Then there was a rock, which he split open, and there was a worm in it. He said to him: 'O Dawud! Your Lord says to you: I hear the voice of this one in the belly of this rock at the bottom of this sea. So did you think that the voice of one who speaks would be hidden from Me?'

key_terms.دُودَةٌ: A worm/larva, representing a small creature

ai.seo_question: What lesson did Prophet Dawud learn about God's hearing from the story of the worm in the rock?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Al-Kafi*, Prophet Dawud (peace be upon him) ascends a mountain at Arafat during Hajj, perhaps seeking solitude or fearing his voice might be lost in the crowd, but God corrects this subtle assumption of concealment. Through Jibra'il, God demonstrates His absolute omniscience by revealing He hears the faintest sound of a worm inside a rock at the bottom of the sea, affirming that no voice is hidden from Him. This event underscores the Shia scholarly emphasis on *Ilm al-Ghayb* (Knowledge of the Unseen) belonging exclusively to God, even for the Prophets, and serves as a spiritual lesson for pilgrims to maintain sincerity (*Ikhlas*) rather than seeking physical isolation for worship.
